Legitimacy research, in most of its empirical forms, assumes a shared referent: that "the law," "the rule," "the right" mean roughly the same thing to everyone being asked whether it is legitimate. My work tests the alternative — that these terms are organised into distinct cultural schemas, unevenly distributed across a population, and that which schema a person holds predicts what they do (report to the police, file a complaint, comply, stay silent) at least as well as their attitudes do.

Kazakhstan is a methodologically useful place to ask this. Russian- and Kazakh-speaking citizens live under one legal system; cohorts who came of age under different legal orders sit side by side. That gives the question empirical traction it wouldn't have in a more homogeneous setting.

Empirically, I work across NLP and embeddings, silicon sampling, survey design, spatial statistics and GIS, and explainable machine learning — in R, Python, SQL and QGIS — grounded in more than a hundred in-depth interviews.

**How this fits together?** My first publication, in 2020, was a review of Eugen Ehrlich on living law — the question behind it was where law exists outside the statute book. The several years of work that followed, on policing, surveillance and victimization, were not driven by an interest in crime as such: crime is where classification is dense, consequential and recorded, which makes it observable. That work produced a methodological objection. Research on legal legitimacy explains compliance through attitudes toward law while assuming the referent is the same for everyone asked; if "law" means different things to different people, measured variation in legitimacy conflates variation in attitude with variation in referent. The current programme follows from that: cognitive sociology supplies the theory of what differs — schemas, unevenly distributed — and computational methods supply the means to measure it.

## Currently working on

- **Schemas of law and order** — testing whether "law," "rule" and "right" function as separate cognitive schemas, using European Social Survey data and the text of citizens' complaints to government bodies. I am extending the same question to the Moral Machine Experiment data, and preparing an experiment of my own designed around it.
- **Prosody and the structure of talk about crime** — an automated pipeline for computational conversation-analytic transcription of calls about crime.
- **Open-ended questions in silicon sampling surveys** — with Daniil Lebedev and Sanzhar Kalkanbay, a factorial field experiment (Astana, N ≈ 1,000) testing whether open-ended items reduce the uniformity bias LLM-simulated respondents show on closed questions. The point is to get a sharper read on how models are biased when the subject is law, rules and order.
